claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: Every Python value has a data type (such as int, float, or str); expressions combine values, and conversion functions move a value from one type to another.
The interpreter performs implicit type conversion to promote types automatically inside a mixed expression.
int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3.
True division (/) converts numbers to floats before dividing and always returns a float.
Floor division (//) computes the whole-number quotient, discarding the remainder.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §2.2 Type conversion; §2.5 Dividing integers

artifact.df: The automatic type promotion performed by the interpreter within a mixed expression.
artifact.eg: A mixed expression involving an int and a float will result in a float.
artifact.mi: Assuming the interpreter only performs explicit type changes when functions are called.
artifact.cx: Recognizing that the interpreter performs implicit type conversion to promote types automatically inside a mixed expression.

artifact.df: An integer-style quotient that drops any remainder.
artifact.eg: In `7 // 2`, the result is `3`, which is the whole-number quotient.
artifact.mi: It means dividing and then rounding to the nearest whole number.
artifact.cx: The operation discards the remainder rather than rounding; the related decimal-producing operator is `/`.

claims: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.
Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.
Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §10.1 Dictionary basics

artifact.df: The constraint that every identifier used to access a stored item must be distinct.
artifact.eg: Ensuring that in a dictionary, no two entries share the same label.
artifact.mi: Assuming that the structure can accommodate multiple entries with the same label.
artifact.cx: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.

artifact.df: A label used to retrieve one stored value from a mapping.
artifact.eg: In a dictionary of course rooms, 'BIO101' can point to one room assignment.
artifact.mi: A key can repeat many times for the same mapping entry.
artifact.cx: Because lookup uses labels, the same key cannot be duplicated in one dictionary.

claims: A function is a named, reusable block of code defined with def that runs only when it is called; variables created inside it are local to that call.
A function is defined with the def keyword, a name, parentheses, and a colon, with an indented body.
A variable's scope is the part of the program where it can be accessed.
A variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function.
A variable created outside any function has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §6.1 Defining functions; §6.3 Variable scope

artifact.q: In a small Python program, a student defines a helper with def, creates a variable inside that helper, and then tries to use that same variable after the call ends. Which statement best describes what happens?
op: It has local scope, so it cannot be accessed outside the function.
It becomes global scope after the function finishes running.
It is available anywhere because it was defined with def.
It can be accessed only from other functions in the program.
artifact.ex: Correct: variables created inside a function have local scope and cannot be accessed outside that function. The common misconception is that a name defined during a call becomes available everywhere after the call, but scope does not work that way.

artifact.q: Which statement accurately describes the scope of a variable defined within a function?
op: It has global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.
It has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function.
It is accessible globally if defined with the def keyword.
It has the same scope as variables defined outside any function.
artifact.ex: The correct choice is that a variable created inside a function has local scope and cannot be accessed outside the function. The misconception is believing that variables defined inside a function retain global scope, which is incorrect.

claims: A volcano's eruptive style is set largely by magma viscosity, which rises with silica content: runny low-silica magma erupts gently, while sticky high-silica magma traps gas and erupts explosively.
Low-viscosity (low-silica, basaltic) magma flows easily like syrup, producing the gentle eruptions of Hawaiian shield volcanoes.
High-viscosity (high-silica, felsic) magma is thick and sticky and flows slowly like toothpaste, trapping gas until it erupts violently.
The most dangerous volcanic hazard is the pyroclastic flow, a fast cloud of hot ash and gas typical of explosive high-silica volcanoes.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4.4 Volcanic eruptions and hazards

artifact.q: What hazard is most characteristic of explosive high-silica volcanoes?
op: Lava flow
Pyroclastic flow
Gentle effusion
Syrup-like flow
artifact.ex: The most dangerous volcanic hazard is the pyroclastic flow, a fast cloud of hot ash and gas typical of explosive high-silica volcanoes. (Misconception: Lava flow is the most dangerous hazard.)

artifact.q: A volcano is fed by magma that moves easily and produces gentle eruptions. Which magma type best fits that description?
op: Basaltic, low-silica magma
Felsic, high-silica magma
A gas-poor ash cloud
A cooled lava dome
artifact.ex: Low-silica magma has low viscosity, so it flows easily and tends to erupt gently. The tempting misconception is that any magma that erupts is sticky; in fact, the stickiest, most explosive magma is the high-silica kind.

claims: The rock cycle describes how Earth's three rock families — igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic — form and continually transform into one another through geologic processes.
The rock cycle describes the major Earth materials, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other.
Igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid; lithified sediment becomes sedimentary rock; pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock.
If conditions melt the rocks into magma, the cycle begins anew with new igneous rocks.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4 The rock cycle

artifact.df: Rock created when liquid rock freezes solid into a solid state.
artifact.mi: Thinking all rocks must be sedimentary.
artifact.cx: Igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid; lithified sediment becomes sedimentary rock; pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock.

artifact.df: Sediment that has been turned into rock by compaction and cementation.
artifact.eg: Sand laid down in layers becomes sandstone after lithification.
artifact.mi: Any sediment near water is already sedimentary rock.
artifact.cx: Sediment must be lithified before it counts as sedimentary rock; loose sediment is not yet rock.

claims: In music, a triad is a set of three notes (or "pitch classes") that can be stacked vertically in thirds.
A seventh chord is a chord consisting of a triad plus a note forming an interval of a seventh above the chord's root.
The seventh destabilized the triad, and allowed the composer to emphasize movement in a given direction.
There are four different inversions of a seventh chord.

artifact.df: The movement or progression of sounds within a piece of music.
artifact.eg: The movement emphasized by a seventh chord.
artifact.mi: The static arrangement of notes in a chord.
artifact.cx: The direction in which a seventh chord emphasizes movement.

artifact.df: A chord built from a triad with one additional note a seventh above the root.
artifact.eg: A chord like C-E-G-B is an example of this type.
artifact.cx: The name refers to the added seventh interval, not to the number of notes in the chord.

claims: In Western musical notation, the staff (UK usually stave); (plural: staves), also occasionally referred to as a pentagram, is a set of horizontal lines (usually five) with spaces between them, that each represent a different musical pitch.
Which staff positions represent which notes is determined by a clef placed at the beginning of the staff.
A clef (from French: clef 'key') is a musical symbol used to indicate which notes are represented by the lines and spaces on a musical staff.
The treble clef is also the upper staff of the grand staff used for harp and keyboard instruments.
Bass clef is the bottom clef in the grand staff for harp and keyboard instruments.

artifact.q: What is the primary function of a clef in Western musical notation?
op: To define the horizontal lines on the staff.
To indicate which notes are represented by the lines and spaces.
To determine the pitch of the spaces on the staff.
To show the relationship between different musical pitches.
artifact.ex: The correct choice indicates that a clef is a symbol used to indicate which notes are represented by the lines and spaces on a musical staff. The misconception is that a clef defines the horizontal lines, which is incorrect; the lines and spaces represent the pitches.

artifact.q: What tells a reader which notes the lines and spaces on a musical staff represent?
op: The clef placed at the beginning
The number of measures in the piece
The tempo marking above the staff
The key signature at the end
artifact.ex: The clef is correct because it is placed at the beginning of the staff and indicates which notes the lines and spaces stand for. A common misconception is to treat the tempo or key signature as the sign that assigns staff positions, but the provided claims assign that job to the clef.

claims: In music theory, an interval is a difference in pitch between two sounds.
In physical terms, an interval is the ratio between two sonic frequencies.
Intervals between successive notes of a scale are also known as scale steps.

artifact.q: What is the term for the intervals between successive notes of a scale?
op: Scale steps
Chord roots
Beat groups
Key signatures
artifact.ex: The correct choice is scale steps because successive notes in a scale are linked by intervals. A plausible misconception is to pick key signatures or chord roots, since both are music terms, but neither names the interval-to-next-note relationship in a scale.

artifact.q: How are the relationships between successive notes of a scale referred to in music theory?
op: A. Intervals between successive notes.
B. Scale steps.
C. Ratios between two sonic frequencies.
D. Differences in pitch between two sounds.
artifact.ex: Option B is correct because intervals between successive notes of a scale are also known as scale steps (Claim 2). Option A is a general term, while Option C describes a physical measurement.

claims: Accessibility and usability evaluation combines standards-based conformance checks with observation of representative users completing realistic tasks.
WCAG organizes web accessibility around the principles perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust.
Evaluation with disabled and older users can find barriers that conformance evaluation alone does not reveal.
A usability test observes users attempting to use a product or service while thinking aloud.
A single disabled participant's experience should not be generalized to all people with disabilities.
sourceContext.license: W3C Document License and U.S. Government Work

artifact.q: During a usability test, which procedure fits the method described in the source?
op: Watch users try the product while they think aloud
Ask users to list every accessibility rule they know
Measure whether the code matches a design system
Have a researcher predict which feature each user will prefer
artifact.ex: Correct: a usability test observes users attempting to use a product or service while thinking aloud. The closest misconception is that testing is mainly about checking rules or predicting preferences; those do not provide the same task-based observation.

artifact.q: What is a limitation of relying solely on conformance evaluation?
op: It fails to check standards.
It misses barriers found by disabled or older users.
It is sufficient for all users.
It only observes users without thinking aloud.
artifact.ex: It misses barriers found by disabled or older users is correct because evaluation with disabled and older users can find barriers that conformance evaluation alone does not reveal (Claim 2).

claims: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective so a team can see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
A journey map should start from research about the steps users actually take and the transactions involved.
An experience map should make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.
A map can reveal dead ends where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.
Journey analysis should include gaps between online and offline parts of a service.

artifact.q: After mapping a checkout journey, the team wants the map to help decide where to improve. What should the map make visible?
op: User struggle points and candidate improvement areas
Only the most successful moments in the service
The team's intended brand story for the service
Hidden motives behind each user's choices
artifact.ex: Correct: the map should surface struggle points and possible improvements. A plausible misconception is that a journey map is mainly a promotional story or a way to infer motives; the source only supports making problems and opportunities visible.

artifact.q: When creating an experience map, what should be made visible?
op: Only the successful paths users take.
Struggle points and candidate improvement areas.
The exact technical specifications of the service.
The final, desired outcome only.
artifact.ex: The correct choice highlights the need to identify areas for enhancement, unlike the misconception that the map only focuses on successful paths.
